quotes.text: McCartney's acquired habitus wasn't just concerned with how to play his chosen instruments fluidly but included learning to work as a professional, including the values, the behaviour expected of a performing musician.
McCartney's domain acquisition as a record producer appeared to develop through a process of osmosis, simply by being fully immersed into studio practice.
the Rodgers and Hammerstein of pop at work
Stop right there. I'm not the person who instigated the split.
John walked into the room one day and said, 'I'm leaving The Beatles.' Is that not instigating the split?
The only way I could fight was in suing the other Beatles, because they were going with Klein. And they thanked me for it, years later. But I didn't instigate the split. That was our Johnny.
One of my great memories is hearing Mum in the kitchen, whistling. I thought 'It's great. Mum's happy.'
In the 60s, when I was doing too much of everything, like all my friends: drugs, drink, whatever… I went to sleep one night and she came to me in a dream.

I was obviously looking a bit wrecked and she was concerned. She said to me, 'Don't worry, it's all going to be all right… just let it be.' I woke up feeling great, having been with my mum, and thought, 'Wait a minute, let it be? That's a great thing. Maybe write a song about it.'
It was years later that somebody said, 'Do you think that's about your mum?' I realised it probably was. At the time, I was just thinking [it was about] a girlfriend.

I had a brilliant English literature teacher called Alan Durban. He got me to get interested [in writing] by telling me about The Miller's Tale [by Geoffrey Chaucer]. When I read it, I thought, 'This is great. It's really dirty.' And it gave me a lot of respect for Chaucer and then it got me interested in other bits of literature.
I did Hamlet and Henry V. At one point, I was thinking I'd love to direct a couple of plays. Hamlet was one. I'd be hopeless!

John lived in Woolton and his friend Ivan was my best friend at school. We just chatted. I knew a couple of songs I could do and I knew all the lyrics, which was very impressive. John was doing stuff he didn't know all the lyrics to and he was just making them up, which I found very impressive. I thought he was pretty cool for that.
This was before The Beatles. We were just hanging out, writing our early songs. We started this play.

I thought that was lost. It's quite a funny little thing. It's called Pilchard and it's about the Messiah. It was in the era of the kitchen sink [drama]. The idea was the mother and the daughter are in the kitchen area… and they're just talking. The mother says, 'Where's Pilchard?' And the daughter says, 'He's upstairs again'… The idea was the whole story would go on and on and it was the Messiah, and that's why he never came down.
I'll go, 'What would John think of this?' and sort of imagine playing it to him.
